match.reason: No bank point teaches solving linear equations needing up to three inverse operations with brackets at Stage 5; the closest, mat-solving-linear-equations, is a Year 11 card with a different depth and only covers simple one- and two-step cases, while the simultaneous and parametric points teach different ideas.

draft.title: Three-step equations
card: To solve an equation, undo each operation with its inverse, and do the same to both sides. Adding and subtracting undo each other. Multiplying and dividing undo each other.
Undo the adding or subtracting first, then the multiplying or dividing. With a bracket, divide both sides by the number outside it, then undo the rest.
Put \(x = 5\) back in: \(2(5 + 3) - 4 = 16 - 4 = 12\). It matches, so the answer is right.
draft.remember: Undo the adding or subtracting first, then the multiplying or dividing, doing the same to both sides.

a.why: Subtract 5: \(3(x - 2) = 15\). Divide by 3: \(x - 2 = 5\), so \(x = 7\). The tempting \(x = 3\) comes from subtracting 2 instead of adding it back.

b.q: Liam solves \(4(x + 1) - 6 = 14\). His first line is \(4(x + 1) = 8\). What did he do wrong, and what is the correct solution?
opts: He subtracted 6 instead of adding it; \(x = 4\)
He subtracted 6 instead of adding it; \(x = 1\)
He added 6 but should have subtracted it; \(x = 4\)
b.why: The \(-6\) is undone by adding 6, giving \(4(x + 1) = 20\). Dividing by 4 gives \(x + 1 = 5\), so \(x = 4\). Using \(x = 1\) follows from his wrong line \(4(x + 1) = 8\), so it keeps his error.

b.best: He subtracted 6 instead of adding it; \(x = 4\)
